name: Thymosin alpha-1
evidenceNote: Several randomized human trials exist, in hepatitis B and in sepsis, but most were open-label or single-blind, and the largest and best-designed one, a 1,106-patient phase 3 sepsis trial, found no effect on survival.
summary: A 28-amino-acid thymus peptide used abroad for hepatitis B and as an immune booster. Not FDA-approved; its largest trial found no survival benefit.
keyTakeaway: Thymosin alpha-1 is a 28-amino-acid peptide first isolated from calf thymus in 1977, and a synthetic version is approved in more than 35 countries, mainly for hepatitis B and C. Randomized trials in hepatitis B reported higher rates of viral clearance than no treatment. In sepsis, a small trial hinted at fewer deaths, but a 2025 phase 3 trial in 1,106 adults found 28-day mortality of 23.4% against 24.1% on placebo. It is not FDA-approved, and an FDA advisory panel voted against allowing pharmacies to compound it.

blocks.text: Thymosin alpha-1 is a short protein chain of 28 amino acids that occurs naturally in the thymus, the gland behind the breastbone where T cells (a type of white blood cell) mature [2]. The drug version is made synthetically and is known by the generic name thymalfasin [3].

It is described as an immunomodulator, a substance that adjusts how the immune system responds rather than attacking a germ directly [1]. Outside the United States it is approved in more than 35 countries to treat hepatitis B and C and as an immune stimulant or vaccine adjuvant (an add-on that strengthens the response to a vaccine) [1]. In the US it is not an approved medicine.

Allan Goldstein and colleagues studied thymosin fraction 5, a mixture of peptides extracted from calf thymus. In 1977 they isolated one of its components, worked out its full amino acid sequence, and named it thymosin alpha-1 [2]. A synthetic version followed, and by the late 1990s it was being tested in randomized trials for chronic hepatitis B [3].

blocks.text: The original work placed thymosin alpha-1 among the thymus peptides that may guide how T cells develop and function [2]. Later laboratory studies pointed to a second route. In laboratory and mouse experiments, it made dendritic cells, the immune cells that present pieces of a germ to T cells, mature and release interleukin-12, a signal that steers the immune system toward fighting infections [4].

That effect ran through toll-like receptors, sensors that detect microbes, and the MyD88 signaling pathway [4]. In mice given bone marrow transplants, the peptide sped the recovery of white blood cells and protected the animals from a lung infection with the mould Aspergillus [4]. How closely these lab findings explain what happens in patients is not settled.

No. Thymosin alpha-1 has never been approved by the FDA for any use. The 2009 review that counts approvals in more than 35 countries also noted late-stage US testing for hepatitis C and melanoma at that time, but none of it led to a US approval [1].

Compounding has been contested. The FDA once placed it in its category of compounding substances that may carry significant safety risks, citing possible immune reactions and too little safety information; the nomination was later withdrawn [9]. At a December 4, 2024 meeting, the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 17 to 4 against adding both forms of the peptide to the 503A bulks list, with several members saying they saw no convincing evidence of effectiveness for the uses under review [8].

In late October 2026, HHS announced it would not act against pharmacies compounding six peptides, BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500, while formal rulemaking continues [12][10]. Thymosin alpha-1 was not one of them.

The strongest support comes from chronic hepatitis B. In a 1998 Taiwanese trial, 98 patients were randomized to 26 weeks of injections, 52 weeks of injections, or no treatment [3]. Eighteen months after starting, the virus and its e antigen (a marker of active replication) had cleared in 40.6% of the 26-week group against 9.4% of untreated patients, and biopsies showed less liver inflammation [3]. A Japanese trial of 316 patients compared two dose levels without a placebo arm and found similar response rates for both [7].

rows: Complete viral response 40.6% (26 weeks) vs 9.4% untreated
ALT normal in 36.4% at 72 weeks; no placebo group

blocks.text: Sepsis, a dangerous whole-body reaction to infection, was the next test. The 2013 ETASS trial in six Chinese hospitals reported fewer deaths at 28 days with thymosin alpha-1, but the difference was borderline and the trial was not double-blind [5]. The TESTS trial then randomized 1,106 adults at 22 centres to injections every 12 hours for seven days or a placebo [6]. Death rates were nearly identical, and no secondary or safety outcome differed between groups [6].

A 2025 meta-analysis of 11 sepsis trials found lower mortality when all were pooled, but the benefit vanished when only high-quality or multicentre trials were counted, and the authors judged the total sample too small for a firm answer [11]. Across these trials side effects were mild, mostly fluctuations in liver enzymes in the hepatitis studies [7]. Wellness uses such as general immune support, long COVID, or anti-aging have not been tested in randomized trials.
